item.title: Lets talk about “Home”
item.dc:creator: Sarana
item.content:encoded:
Understanding place, belonging, and identity

As a Doctor of Applied Health Research and data scientist, my career has been built on translating complex patterns into human-centred solutions. After years of bridging clinical data and patient experiences in UK cancer services, I’ve developed a singular curiosity:

How do we narrate our own lives?

Follow as I experiment with applying analytical rigor to the architecture of everyday life, exploring how we build identity and belonging when we leave traditional, fixed structures behind.

What this project is

Ideas of home and belonging shape how people understand themselves and the places they inhabit. For travellers, the meaning of home can shift depending on movement, community, culture, and lived experience.

Bringing together data science and lived experience, I have developed a strong interest in how people narrate and make sense of their lives. This project is an experiment in extending that curiosity into everyday life and travel.

I'm interviewing people to explore how they understand belonging, identity, and home, and how these ideas change over time. This is part of an ongoing journey into how we narrate our own lives.

Who I'm talking to

Phase 1: In progress

Travellers

Portable versions of home.
Temporary routines.
Familiarity built through movement.

Demographics from all 25 travellers interviewed so far

Country of origin

Age

Phase 2: Upcoming comparative enquiry

Rootedness

Community

People in between

Volunteers

Seasonal residents,

People negotiating multiple versions of belonging.

Every conversation so far has been with a traveller (not yet a local or someone in between). More on what that means below ↓

How a conversation works

Conversations happen casually over coffee or in shared spaces.

They move through memories, places, routines, and the different ways people experience home, carry belonging, and experience place across movement and change.

Some questions I keep coming back to:

Exploration
How much do you find vs create home?
Evolution
Has your idea of home changed over time?
Perception
Is "home" more of a feeling or a place to you?

How I make sense of it all

There is a method to storytelling magic! To find the deeper patterns in these travel and lifestyle experiences, conversation data goes through a rigorous (but highly visual) thematic analysis.

I record each conversation, listen back for patterns, group similar ideas together, and slowly build shared themes across everyone I've spoken to.

This doodle diagram illustrates my path from raw audio and rough notes to the final narratives and galleries emerging.

The Travellers gallery: everyone's word, colour, and shape

At the end of each interview, once we were fully immersed in the conversation, I captured participants’ intuitive sense of home as a word, colour, and shape. To me, these are visual fingerprints of belonging.

The following gallery serves as a living record of every individual who took part in an interview with me. By turning each person’s story into a unique visual card, I can:

  1. Organise individual experiences into larger, shared themes.
  2. Keep the project open and connected, allowing participants to see their own experiences reflected in the emerging collective story. As the project grows, those who shared their stories remain at the heart of the work.

Person-cards are currently organised by two layers:

  1. The single word each person landed on at the end of our conversation (after being deliberately guided there)
  2. How people talked about home earlier in the conversation, in their own unprompted words.

These sometimes differ. This is what I like to think of as the gap between a considered final answer and in-the-moment thinking.

Note: A dashed border means a tag is my own interpretive read rather than something said outright.

Try sorting the gallery by how each person described home

The final word

Stay tuned to see how I continue to curate and group these into the evolving themes of the project!

Headline findings: Travellers

Eight traveller "stories" stand out. Each story is drawn from thematic analysis across every conversation to date.

Click through to see what's actually behind each one.

Nine in ten reach for a feeling, not a building.

Nearly everyone I've asked reduces home to a feeling, a person, or something shared - safe, loved, warmth, peace - rather than a location. Only one person names an actual place, and that's not incidental: his is the one story built around loss, where home is somewhere that no longer exists to go back to.

25 of 26 conversations coded.
Comfort has almost nothing to do with it.

When somewhere doesn't feel like home, it's almost never the building's fault. A flat that ticked every box on paper still didn't work. A beautiful, empty hostel didn't either. For a few women specifically, feeling genuinely safe, not just comfortable, has been the deciding factor - and one participant's genuinely hard physical day (illness, heat, a dying phone) didn't dent her sense of belonging at all, because the people around her didn't let her down.

17 of 26 conversations coded.
"Both" means something different for nearly everyone.

Asked directly whether they find home or create it, most land on some version of both - but that word covers real variety. For some it's inseparable. For others it splits cleanly by place and time. For one person, it's not even the right question anymore.

18 of 26 conversations coded.
For one person, the question doesn't even apply anymore.

Most people can answer whether they find or create home. One can't, because the place it would refer to doesn't exist to go back to. His response wasn't either option - it was choosing not to call anywhere home at all, so he can't lose it again.

A single, clean, well-corroborated case.
One in four didn't grow up with just one home.

A real minority didn't have a single, stable childhood home. Some held two at once, moving between separated parents. Two people, independently, pictured a holiday flat or a weekend house before their actual childhood home - because it was the place free of whatever was harder there.

19 of 26 conversations coded.
Home and hardship turn out to be close neighbours.

This started as a project about travel. Close to a third of the people I've spoken to in depth have opened up about real difficulty - family history, loss, things people don't always get asked about directly. I didn't expect that. I think it says something true.

9 of 27 conversations read in depth.
Some languages don't separate house from home at all.

For a few multilingual participants, home isn't just described differently in each language - it's built differently. Polish and French don't distinguish "house" from "home." Spanish does, like English. A few people have needed a different language entirely to find the right word.

3 of 21 conversations read in depth - small, but consistent.
New places don't just permit reinvention. They reward it.

A few people chose unfamiliar places specifically because nobody there had an old idea of who they were. One took it further: in a brand-new group, people who are themselves unsure are drawn to whoever seems confident and different - so starting over doesn't just allow reinvention, it can actively select for it.

3 of 27 conversations read in depth.

This full analysis draws from every conversation collected with travellers across the project.

Live update:outdated (delete later)

I’ve mapped general patterns, the emotional tone, contradictions and gut reactions across stories.

“9 in 10 reach for a feeling or a person rather than a building.”

Almost nobody describes home as a place. More than nine in ten reach for a feeling (safe, loved, warmth, peace) or for a person, or for something they do together, rather than a building or a location. Only one person in the set so far names an actual, specific place, and it's not a coincidence: theirs is the one story built around loss, where home is somewhere that no longer exists to go back to.

“Comfort, it turns out, has very little to do with it.”

When someone tells me about somewhere that didn't feel like home, it's almost never about the physical space. A flat that ticked every box on paper. A beautiful, empty hostel. A city that wasn't unsafe, but not somewhere they fit. For a few women in the group specifically, feeling genuinely safe (not just comfortable) has been the deciding factor. Comfort, it turns out, has very little to do with it.

“'Both' means something different for nearly everyone.”

Asked directly whether people find home or create it, most land on some version of both, although "both" means something different for nearly everyone. For some it's inseparable, for others it splits cleanly by place and time, and for at least one person the question doesn't quite apply anymore, because the home it would be about doesn't exist to be found or created.

“A linguistic texture of belonging.”

For some, there is a linguistic texture of belonging that is more than relationships or affect. Polish and French do not distinguish "house" from "home" at all. Spanish (like English), does.

“Home and hardship turn out to be closer neighbours than we assume.”

A good number of these conversations have opened onto real difficulty such as family history, loss, things people don't always get asked about directly. I hadn't expected a project about travel to open that door so often. I think it says something true: home and hardship turn out to be closer neighbours than we assume.

This full analysis draws from every conversation collected with travellers across the project.

What this can (and can't) tell you

A note on me

I'm not a neutral outsider asking these questions. I live in this community too. Every conversation ends with a debrief, where I share a little of what I'm noticing across the project so far. This is partly because people are genuinely curious what happens with what they've told me, and partly because it felt wrong to take without giving something back. That means the person I'm talking to isn't just a source of data. By the end of each conversation, they know a bit about the emerging picture too, and that is deliberate.

My own move from structured clinical research into this project is itself part of the story I'm telling. So read every "pattern" on this page as filtered through someone who's inside the thing she's describing, and who talks to her participants about it too. I'm not observing from a clean, silent distance.

A note on who I've spoken to (and who I haven't yet)

Phase 1 of this project (the 25 conversations behind everything on this page so far) all come from one place: Wonderland, a mobile volunteer community. That's not incidental to what I'm finding. Anyone who signs up to volunteer their way around the world has probably already made peace with home not being fixed to one address, so it's worth holding my headline finding that home is overwhelmingly a feeling, not a place, as true for people who've already chosen mobility, rather than a universal claim about everyone. I'd expect a different starting point from someone who's never left their hometown.

I also set out to speak to three groups: travellers, locals, and people in between. So far, every conversation has been with a traveller. The "locals" and "people in between" categories on this page are still aspirational, not yet backed by data. That's the next phase, not a finished comparison.

Finally, not every conversation has been coded on every dimension yet. The headline stat (that roughly 9 in 10 people reach for a feeling rather than a place) is drawn from all 25 conversations. Some of the more detailed patterns (how people find versus create home, what breaks the feeling of it for them) are currently based on 15–16 of the 25.

How I'm starting to organise what I'm hearing

The honest shape of what I'm finding isn't neat categories. It's closer to one dominant pattern with real texture underneath it. The overwhelming majority of people so far (more than 9 in 10) land somewhere in the relational and emotional register when you ask them what home really is.

Underneath that, there's genuine variety in how people carry or rebuild that feeling while they're on the move. It could be a particular tea, a comfort show, fairy lights strung up in a new room, or sometimes nothing physical at all, just the right people nearby. And then there's a small, powerful handful of stories where home isn't something to find or build anymore, because the place it would refer to doesn't exist to go back to.

So rather than sorting people into boxes, I'm holding onto one dominant pattern, the many different ways people enact it, and the exceptions that show what happens when it isn't available at all. That feels truer to what's actually in front of me than any tidy structure would.

Where will this go?

Envisaged outputs include: data driven art and creative storytelling

What I'm loving so far!

Pause & Reflect

Conversations become spaces to pause and open up honest dialogue.

Connection

Sharing stories connects me cross-culturally through curiosity.

Research Shift

Moving from science to creative human storytelling.

Redefining Home

Finding insights into how people create and carry home.

Emerging feedback

“It’s been gorgeous...I didn’t expect the conversation to be so emotional. I know that I have a solid sense of home...It’s been really amazing to unpack what that foundation means for me, I hadn’t really thought about it this deeply before so thank you.”

“I love the questions you asked me. It was really helpful, really nice... I just really think that it's nice that we appreciate home as a feeling. Because that also means that you can technically be home everywhere you are.”

“lalalalal.”

item.title: How to ̶b̶e̶ make a mermaid
item.dc:creator: Sarana
item.content:encoded:
Creating a monument to childhood autonomy: the vision, the grit, and the reflection.

Something has always drawn me to the sea. I grew up in London where every-day access comes from stories, imagination, encyclopaedias, and documentaries (narrated by David Attenborough). Ever since I was a child, I was obsessed with legends of mermaids. I wrote and made my own version of “The little mermaid” because I was just so annoyed that the little mermaid turned her back on her entire species for a man! Despite spending a lot of time in Sri Lanka as a child, most of this time was spent with family in the Capital city of Colombo. That being said, I have treasured memories of rare, huge, extended family trips to the south coast of Mirissa where we played in the sea constantly.

Neither obsession disappeared as an adult. The dangerous thing about being me is that in many ways I’m still my child version but equipped with full autonomy and adult resources. Maybe that is why life drops me onto tropical horizons like Siquijor. It isn't just picturesque; it is a legendary Philippine island of mysticism and magic. It’s a place where the air feels heavy with old secrets, and if mermaids were real, this is 100% the coastline they would claim.

When I first arrived in Wonderland, I had a million artistic ideas. Writing and painting is my comfort zone; it’s what I know I can do well while on the move (think watercolour journaling and writing short stories). But in Wonderland, the constraints of moving didn’t exist. I wanted to challenge myself, to push past the familiar and see what happened. I wanted to fully utilize the seemingly abundant resources around me that I would otherwise never have access to in normal life. The workshop felt like an unregulated playground with power tools at everyone’s disposal, and there was absolutely nothing stopping me from testing them out. I spent about a week sussing out the space and its capabilities, throwing myself into bamboo construction first just to test the limits of what was possible (and feel like Lara Croft wielding a machete).

As I scoped out the space, a creative vision iteratively formed and I pitched the basic idea to management: I wanted to create a mermaid art installation. I called it mermaiding, or more formally, a 2.5D art installation.

It was through the act of doing that I began to realise what I was capable of. I learned how to build, scale, and measure from an engineering and design perspective, simply because the piece demanded it. I figured out the circular saw and the jigsaw by using them with the help of new friends. I explored the island for organic materials because I needed textures and wanted artistic immortality. I changed my ideas when things didn’t work out to my satisfaction.

I learned that I could saw, hammer and nail stuff.

I could be cute and arrange pretty shells, and feel like an alchemist brewing wood varnish with solvent.

I could weave banana roots into precise braids, and smash glass into random scaley shapes.

I could wear dungarees that had a hundred pockets for spare silicon glue, pencils, and my measurement notebook.

It became a project that perfectly complemented how my brain works. It was entirely hands-on, but also something I could pick up and put down in between helping out at the local dog shelter, primary school, and later, running my personal qualitative project exploring the meaning of home among the other volunteers.

And all the while, it felt like a dual process: I was making a mermaid, but I was becoming one too, every time I swam in tropical waters from my childhood dreams, now sitting on my doorstep.
